Departures & Arrivals
When a population point moves, the settlement it leaves loses a worked tile, the migrants travel for one or more turns, and the settlement they join places the point when they arrive.
Leaving

Each departing point removes one of the settlement's outlying rural improvements and that tile's yields. Pillaged tiles go first. A starving city keeps its food tiles longest. Otherwise plain tiles go before resource tiles, and distant plots before near ones. Cultural Enclave tiles are exempt. The emptied rural district is then cleared so the city can grow onto the tile again.

A settlement loses at most two points per turn on the default Medium preset. A single siege displaces at most 60% of the population the city had when it began, and a single disaster at most 50%. Deaths from a long crisis (see When There Is No Refuge) fall outside these caps.
On the Road

Travel time grows with distance, up to four turns by default, and slower game speeds stretch it. War refugees always spend at least one turn on the road. If their destination is captured or razed while they travel, or stays too full to receive them, they die in transit and count as losses.
A settlement takes in at most four newcomers per turn by default. The rest wait and try again next turn, longest-waiting first.
Arriving

Other civilizations place their own arrivals. For your cities, the How newcomers settle setting (Options, Add-ons, Emigration, Advanced settings, Arrivals & departures) decides what happens:[BLIST][LI][B]Ask me[/B] (default): a Newcomers or Refugees pop-up in the receiving city lets you pick the tile, let the city decide, or wait. Three switches choose which kinds of arrival ask; by default only refugees ask, and migrants and returning people are placed at once.[LI][B]Automatic[/B]: the city places the point immediately, as it does when it grows.[LI][B]Migrant unit[/B]: the newcomers arrive as a Migrant unit beside the city for you to resettle. An unsettled Migrant costs upkeep every turn.[LI][B]Off[/B]: the game's own Grow City prompt asks you to place the point.[/LIST]

The Refugees pop-up names where the arrivals fled from and what they fled, with a quotation in their people's voice (see Voices of the Displaced). Refugees from a civilization you have not met are described only as displaced.
Refugees Waiting to Settle

One in five war and disaster refugees (by default) settles on arrival. The rest enter a waiting pool at their destination and settle over the following turns. A happy, open, uncrowded host settles them faster; an Anti-Immigration Stance slows them. The host pays upkeep for those still waiting. If the crisis they fled reaches the new city, the waiting refugees move on first. The city readout and the City Details panel show how many are waiting.
The Cost of Taking People In

Each newcomer adds an integration load to the receiving civilization, which fades over about six to eight turns. While it lasts, the civilization pays [icon:YIELD_GOLD] Gold each turn and its accumulated [icon:YIELD_HAPPINESS] Happiness is drawn down, delaying its next Celebration. A civilization settling many arrivals also attracts fewer new ones. Each of these costs can be set to 0 in Advanced settings; see Integration & the Cost of Growth.
Calling Your People Home

When none of your settlements is under war, siege, disaster or famine and some of your people still live away from the settlement they fled, the mod offers a call to bring them home. The dialog opens with a homecoming quotation in your people's voice (see Voices of the Displaced) and takes one of two forms, depending on where the people are. If you decline, they stay where they are and may still return on their own over time.
From Your Own Settlements

For people in another of your settlements, the call is a purchase: choose how many, pay, and that many return, largest group first. The dialog names the settlement they leave and the one they return to.
From Foreign Cities

For people in another civilization's city, the call is a gamble. The dialog names the city and its ruler and shows the chance that each person answers (about 18% by default). Each person is rolled separately, and you pay for the size you chose whatever the result. An unanswered call is written into the Chronicle and starts the cooldown.
Prices and Cooldowns

Each call offers three sizes, one person, about half of those callable, and everyone, in [icon:YIELD_GOLD] Gold or [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence, showing only the sizes you can afford. Price rises faster than head count: two people cost nearly three times one, three about five times. Calls abroad cost more, and each age past Antiquity multiplies the price (x3 in the Exploration Age, x9 in the Modern Age). After a call, the same civilization waits eight turns before calling again.
A community with a Cultural Enclave rarely returns on its own, so a call is the reliable way to bring it back. The offer, prices and odds are set under Calling people home in Advanced settings.
Immigration Policies

Emigration adds policy cards to the civics of every age. They slot and swap like any other card and stack with an Open Borders agreement, which raises migration both ways between the two signatories. Each card's flat yields are native game effects; its migration effect comes from the mod.
Antiquity Age

[BLIST][LI][B]Pro-Immigration Stance[/B] (Citizenship): +50% immigration; +1 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence each turn.[LI][B]Anti-Immigration Stance[/B] (Citizenship): -60% immigration, 40% fewer of your citizens leave for rival civilizations, and refugees you take in settle more slowly; +2 [icon:YIELD_PRODUCTION] Production in every city, -2 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence each turn.[/LIST]
Exploration Age

[BLIST][LI][B]Pro-Immigration Stance[/B] (Economics): +50% immigration; +2 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence each turn.[LI][B]Anti-Immigration Stance[/B] (Economics): -60% immigration, 40% fewer citizens leave for rivals, refugees settle more slowly; +3 [icon:YIELD_PRODUCTION] Production in every city, -3 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence each turn.[LI][B]Talent Attraction[/B] (Inspiration): +1 [icon:YIELD_SCIENCE] Science each turn, plus about +1.5 for every immigrant you attract, up to +12. The bonus fades when immigration stops.[LI][B]Cultural Magnetism[/B] (Society): the same, in [icon:YIELD_CULTURE] Culture.[LI][B]Commercial Draw[/B] (Mercantilism): the same, in [icon:YIELD_GOLD] Gold.[LI][B]Selective Asylum[/B] (Piety): draws refugees fleeing war and disaster toward you, the most desperate first; +1 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence each turn.[/LIST]
Modern Age

[BLIST][LI][B]Pro-Immigration Stance[/B] (Social Question): +50% immigration; +3 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence each turn.[LI][B]Anti-Immigration Stance[/B] (Social Question): -60% immigration, 40% fewer citizens leave for rivals, refugees settle more slowly; +4 [icon:YIELD_PRODUCTION] Production in every city, -4 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence each turn.[LI][B]Talent Attraction[/B] (Modernization): +2 [icon:YIELD_SCIENCE] Science each turn, plus about +1.5 per immigrant, up to +12, fading when immigration stops.[LI][B]Cultural Magnetism[/B] (Natural History): the same, in [icon:YIELD_CULTURE] Culture.[LI][B]Commercial Draw[/B] (Capitalism): the same, in [icon:YIELD_GOLD] Gold.[LI][B]Refugee Compact[/B] (Political Theory): draws refugees fleeing war and disaster toward you, the most desperate first; +2 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence and +1 [icon:YIELD_CULTURE] Culture each turn.[/LIST]
The attraction cards pay only while people keep arriving. Pair one with a Pro-Immigration Stance, Open Borders or an asylum card, and swap it out when the inflow stops.
Map Lenses

Emigration adds two lenses to the game's lens panel, each with a hotkey. Both follow the Analytics visibility setting (see Scope & Visibility). While a lens is up, the game's tile tooltip is hidden and the lens shows its own readout under the cursor.
Prosperity Lens (Shift+P)

The Prosperity lens paints each settled tile by what stands on it. A tile's score is the sum of:[BLIST][LI]a wonder on the hex: +6[LI]the city centre: +3[LI]each building: +2, and +1 for a completed quarter[LI]a worked improvement: +1[LI]the hex's own yield: +1 per 3[LI]a river: +1[LI]a natural wonder: +3 on the hex, +2 for each next door[LI]a wonder next door: +1 each[LI]anything pillaged: -3 each on the hex, -1 each next door[/LIST]The scale is the same in every settlement and is banded: Flourishing (8 or more), Thriving (5 to 7), Ordinary (2 to 4), Meagre (0 to 1) and Blighted (below 0), on grey-to-green and grey-to-red gradients. Water with nothing built on it is left unpainted.

Hovering a tile shows its band, score and every term behind it, then the settlement's Prosperity score, whether it is gaining or losing people, and why. Wonders and natural wonders are read from the game's database, so ones added by an age or another mod count too.
Ethnic Composition Lens (Shift+E)

Each settlement records the civilization each of its people descends from. The Ethnic Composition lens draws that record as a per-tile mosaic. The urban core takes the dominant origin's colour. Each smaller community gets a number of tiles in proportion to its share, densest tiles first, in a paler colour the smaller it is. A community with a Cultural Enclave is placed on the enclave's tile first. Without an enclave, a tile's colour is capped at the share an enclave requires, so a community below that share shows as a lighter tint. Hover a settled tile for its exact mix.
Enclave Markers

An enclave tile uses the model of the improvement it stands in for, so it carries a marker with the origin civilization's symbol. Hovering the tile shows the enclave's tooltip in place of the improvement's: the enclave's name and stage (established, recognized, contested or fading), the tile's yields and their sources, what the enclave's people built there, what the replaced improvement still pays the city, and the stance the city took when it recognized the enclave.
Notifications & the City Readout
Toasts

Migration events appear as toasts. They stack, stay about eleven seconds, and are coloured by cause: green for people gained in your own cities, and neutral, amber or crisis colours for departures and losses. Counts are shown in population points, in people, or both, for example 3 population points (36,000 people), set by the Population unit of measurement option. Disasters carry the game's event names, wars their names, and conquests the name of the city taken.

By default only the largest event of each migration pass toasts, with cooldowns and thresholds on top. The Notifications section of Advanced settings switches to a toast per cause, or to none. Every notification goes to the log either way.
The Notifications Log

The Notifications tab of the Migration dashboard keeps the last 120 notifications, newest first: the turn, the cause and named event, the settlement people left, where they went, and how many. Each entry expands to its detail. Migration Chronicle entries (an exodus, a diaspora taking root, a homecoming, an enclave recognized or faded, each refugee decision and each call home) appear in the same list.
The City Readout

Selecting one of your cities shows a small migration panel: the pressures on it (unhappiness, war, disaster, famine, overcrowding), whether it is gaining or losing people and how fast, where leavers are likely to go, what its newcomers cost, refugees waiting to settle, progress toward a Cultural Enclave, and a line of advice. A warning marks a city whose people have nowhere to flee.
City Details

The game's City Details panel gains two Emigration sections. Under Citizen Growth: the city's people by origin, emigration by destination, immigration by origin, and refugees awaiting settlement. Under Building Breakdown: the city's Cultural Enclave, if it has one. Both update as you switch cities.
Options & Intensity

Emigration's settings are under Options, Add-ons, in the main menu and in game. The Add-ons tab holds the everyday settings, and the Advanced settings button opens the rest. Changes apply immediately or at the next migration pass.
Intensity Presets

The Intensity preset sets the per-turn limits, how far people travel, and how strongly violence pushes them out.[BLIST][LI][B]Low[/B]: rare, small movements; at most one point out and two in per city per turn; slow siege displacement.[LI][B]Medium[/B] (default): at most two out and four in per city per turn.[LI][B]High[/B]: frequent, large movements; up to four out and eight in per city per turn, faster flight and heavier war surges.[/LIST]Changing a preset-controlled setting in Advanced settings shows the preset as Custom.
Everyday Settings

[BLIST][LI][B]Population unit of measurement[/B]: population points, historically scaled people (matching the Demographics mod), or both.[LI][B]Movement between civilizations[/B] and three [B]Refugees from conflict[/B] sliders (overall, wars between major powers, raids by minor powers) scale those flows alone.[LI][B]Dashboard data[/B]: live migration, or sample data to preview the network. [B]Migration timeline detail[/B]: how often the network records a timeline snapshot. [B]Simplify dashboard[/B]: hides the Network and Causes views. [B]Dashboard dock button[/B].[LI]On/off switches for [B]notifications[/B], [B]ethnic integration[/B], [B]return migration[/B] and [B]refugee decisions[/B].[LI][B]Analytics visibility[/B]: which civilizations the dashboard and lenses show (see Scope & Visibility).[/LIST]
Advanced Settings

The Advanced settings window holds every individual setting, more than a hundred, in collapsible sections: Pacing, Scope, Border policies, Prosperity model, War & violence, Disasters, Geography & movement, Integration costs, Balance brakes, Arrivals & departures, Cultural enclaves, Calling people home, Attrition, Notifications, Readouts & rankings and Visuals. Sections you open stay open. Values show their units (55%, x1.5, 3 turns) or a word (Off, Instant). The window has a search box, a marker on each changed setting, a reset for each, and Reset all. Per-leader and per-civilization tuning (see Leaders & Civilizations) has its own switch here.
Game Speed

Every turn count in the mod scales with game speed, from Online to Marathon: cooldowns, transit time, integration periods, enclave dwell and fade clocks, and decision cooldowns. A Marathon game sees the same migrations spread over proportionally more turns. Population counts stay the same at every speed.
The Demographics Mod

Emigration runs on its own. With the Demographics mod installed, it also adds an Emigration tab to the Demographics screen and shares its population scaling, so a population point means the same number of people in both. The Migration dashboard's tabs appear there as sub-tabs, and the Migration page in Demographics opens the dashboard.
Graphs and Tables

[BLIST][LI][B]Net Migration (Graph)[/B]: cumulative arrivals minus departures, by civilization.[LI][B]Net Migration (Table)[/B]: the same value as a diverging bar, beside departures and arrivals split into Internal (between a civilization's own settlements), External (across a border, which is what Net measures) and Total.[LI][B]Emigration[/B] and [B]Immigration[/B]: gross outflow and inflow, broken down by cause.[LI][B]Refugees (Left / Arrived)[/B]: displaced people sent and received, with optional war and disaster markers on the timeline.[/LIST]A Data section toggles the metrics and the unit (scaled people or population points). Demographics' war-effects tooltip can show a Refugees row from Emigration's numbers.
Voices of the Displaced

Each pop-up about refugees, migrants, a returning diaspora or a settled foreign community carries a short quotation in the voice of that people: a refugee, exile or migrant of theirs where such words survive, otherwise a witness who wrote of them with dignity. Each civilization's page lists its quotations, where each appears, and who the speaker was.
Where the Voices Appear

[BLIST][LI][B]The refugee decision[/B] (Refugees at the Border, The Sick at the Gates) and [B]the Refugees pop-up[/B]: a refugee's words from the people fleeing.[LI][B]The Newcomers pop-up[/B]: a migrant's words from their people.[LI][B]The call-home dialog[/B]: someone of your own civilization who longed for home or came back to it.[LI][B]The Cultural Enclave decision[/B]: a line from the enclave people's own writers, inscriptions or proverbs; a people's first and second enclaves in your empire each have their own line.[/LIST]The event fixes the line, so reloading a save shows the same words. When a people has no line for a situation, or comes from a civilization you have not met, the pop-up uses the general pools on the Voices of Many Lands page, which name no people.
How the Quotations Were Chosen

Every line was checked against a readable copy of its source. Cuts are marked with an ellipsis. A published translation names its translator; (trans.) alone marks the mod's own rendering of the verified original. Enclave lines come from a people's own writers, inscriptions and proverbs. Refugee and migrant lines come from a refugee, exile or migrant of that people, or else a witness who wrote of them with dignity.

Lines that stereotype a people, cast the displaced as invaders, a burden or a threat, quote a perpetrator of atrocities or a hate figure, trivialize sacred text, or dwell on graphic trauma were excluded. The full source record, including rejected lines, is published with the mod's documentation.
Original Languages

A quotation from a non-English source shows the original beside an English rendering. Latin-script originals appear in full, from Old English and Old Norse to Vietnamese, Turkish and the transliterated Akkadian of the Assyrian inscriptions. Originals in Arabic, Hebrew, Greek, Cyrillic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Georgian, Mongolian, the Indic and Southeast Asian scripts, and Chinese, Japanese and Korean are shown in English only, because the game's fonts lack those scripts.
About Emigration

Emigration is a user-interface mod. Each turn it reads the state of the world and writes population, tiles, yields and Influence back through the game's own commands, adding only its own database rows; base-game rules, files and AI decisions are left as they are. It simulates every living major civilization from the first turn, met or unmet. The Guide tab of the Migration dashboard has a one-screen reference of what drives migration.

Version 3.1.1, for Civilization VII 1.5.0. The interface is available in twelve languages. The source, the full documentation with every formula, and the record of every quotation's source are on GitHub at github.com/tmtmiller1/civilizationvii-emigration.
The People Behind the Numbers

This mod turns migration and displacement into game systems. In reality people most often leave home because of war, persecution, disaster or hardship. The mod presents refugees as people, lets the displaced speak in their own words wherever those words survive, and counts a stricken city's losses as deaths. The author has marked the mod's milestones with donations to refugee relief. If you are able, consider supporting UNHCR, the International Rescue Committee, Médecins Sans Frontières, the International Refugee Assistance Project, or local refugee and mutual-aid groups.
Credits

Emigration is by Tower. Its Prosperity model adapts the Emigration mod for Civilization V by Tomahawk, Mk Z and Tim_The_Texan. Population scaling matches the Demographics mod, and the Talent Raid diplomacy actions come from the Diplomacy Extended mod. Quotations are drawn from the published sources listed in the mod's documentation; translations marked (trans.) without a translator's name are the mod's own.
